documents: Deng & Levander (2022), Autocorrelation R2 on Mars, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL099580 (published PDF, 9 pages; Supporting Information not supplied)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (article pages 'n of 9'); Supporting Information figures cited by figure number on the main-text page that reports them

entry.evidence: suggests the potential for a similar analysis for InSight seismic data

steps.action: Take from other groups the single-station low-frequency autocorrelation method that recovers Earth-orbiting Rayleigh waves (R2), and its proposed transfer to InSight data.
steps.quote: This was subsequently extended to extract the Earth orbiting Rayleigh waves from a single-station-based autocorrelation

steps.action: Obtain InSight SEIS continuous data (Feb 2019 to Mar 2021) from IRIS and remove glitches with SEISglitch, then deconvolve the response, filter, rotate to Z-N-E and cut into 584 daily segments.
steps.quote: we applied the open-source Python package SEISglitch (Scholz et al., 2020) to detect and remove the quasi-periodic glitches in the raw SEIS data

steps.action: Test that glitch removal mitigates glitches without introducing artifacts (Figures S2 and S3).
steps.quote: We performed tests to determine that the glitch removal method can mitigate the effects of glitches without introducing additional artifacts

steps.action: Recompute and stack the autocorrelations with 12-hr epochs instead of 1-day epochs to check the phase identification (Figure S4).
steps.quote: We also computed and stacked the autocorrelations using 12-hr epochs

steps.action: Compute daily vertical-component autocorrelograms (0.005-0.01 Hz) after temporal and spectral normalization, select epochs with RMSR_S (508 of 584 kept), and stack linearly and with tf-PWS (power 2).
steps.quote: The daily autocorrelograms were computed by the inverse Fourier transform of the power spectra of the vertical-component ambient noise signals

steps.action: Vary the RMSR_S signal and noise windows (Figure S5) and the tf-PWS exponent (Figure S6); the window tests give almost identical results.
steps.quote: shows tests of different signal and noise window selections in RMSR_S

steps.action: Run a synthetic test of the ability of tf-PWS to enhance coherent signals (Figure S7).
steps.quote: a synthetic test designed to demonstrate the efficiency of tf-PWS to enhance coherent signals

steps.action: Identify a signal at about 6,000 s lag, interpreted as R2, in both linear and tf-PWS stacks; it is clearer with RMSR_S (Figure 1).
steps.quote: A signal that we interpret as the Mars orbiting Rayleigh wave R2 is prominent at ∼6,000 s

steps.action: Run bootstrap stacks on subsets of the data to test the robustness of the R2 identification (Figure S8).
steps.quote: Bootstrap calculations using a subset of the whole data set further suggest the R2 phase identification is robust

steps.action: Measure R2 group velocities between 115 and 200 s by FTAN on the RMSR_S plus tf-PWS stack (Figures 2b and S9).
steps.quote: we applied FTAN (Bensen et al., 2007; Levshin et al., 1992) to calculate the group velocities between 115 and 200 s

steps.action: Compute synthetic group dispersion curves for the Stähler et al. (2021) suite of 1-D models, from mean-3σ to mean+3σ.
steps.quote: We calculated synthetic group velocity dispersion curves for a set of velocity models (Figure 2a)

steps.action: Compare the FTAN group velocities with the model predictions; the observations match the mean-3σ model.
steps.quote: The FTAN-measured group velocities are compatible with the velocity model 3 standard deviations lower than the mean velocity

steps.action: Compute DSM synthetic Green's functions over the range of radii allowed by ellipticity, then convolve them with a source wavelet taken from the autocorrelation near zero lag to make synthetic R2 seismograms for each model.
steps.quote: we simulated and then calculated a weighted mean of the synthetic Green's functions for a range of radii between the polar and equatorial radius

steps.action: Check that the ellipticity-weighted synthetic is almost identical to the mean-radius synthetic (Figure S10).
steps.quote: The mean synthetic was almost identical to the synthetic Green's functions using the mean Martian radius

steps.action: Cross-correlate the observed R2 with each synthetic; time lags are positive down to mean-2σ and change sign at mean-3σ, so the upper mantle is slower than the mean model.
steps.quote: The time lags are positive for velocity models from 3 standard deviations above the mean to 2 standard deviations lower than the mean velocity

steps.action: Run a Monte Carlo inversion from the mean-3σ model over 40-700 km depth (range set by sensitivity kernels): 10 random perturbations per iteration, keep the best fit, stop after 3 iterations when the misfit rises.
steps.quote: For each iteration, we randomly perturbed the starting velocity model 10 times and calculated the DSM

steps.action: Compare the final-model synthetic with the observed R2; the correlation coefficient rises from 0.831 to 0.914 and the time shift falls by a factor of 5 (Figure 3f).
steps.quote: increases the correlation coefficients and reduces the absolute correlation time shifts between the observed and synthetic R2 waveforms by a factor of 5

steps.action: Check that the final model fits independent body-wave traveltime picks made with different picking methods (Figures S14 and S15).
steps.quote: our final model can fit the body wave traveltime picks derived using different picking methods

steps.action: Describe the revised S-wave model: faster than the starting model below 200 km, slower above 200 km, with an LVZ to about 400 km.
steps.quote: the S-wave velocity has been increased compared to the starting model at depths >200 km and is reduced at depths <200 km

steps.action: Set the about-400 km S-wave LVZ against the cited marsquake S-shadow zone, the Khan et al. (2021) geophysical inversion, and the Xu et al. (2021) laboratory velocities, and find them consistent.
steps.quote: consistent with the S-body wave shadow zone observed in the Marsquake data

steps.action: Retain the R2-fitted upper mantle model, with an S-wave LVZ to about 400 km and velocities slower than the Stähler et al. mean model.
steps.quote: The S-wave LVZ extends to a depth of ∼400 km in the Martian upper [...]

tree.answer: Yes: an R2 arrival at about 6,000 s in the stacked InSight autocorrelations
No: mantle velocity is inferred by fitting synthetics to R2
Constrain the 1-D Martian upper mantle velocity (40-700 km)
A suite of Stähler et al. (2021) 1-D models, mean-3σ to mean+3σ
Yes: synthetic dispersion curves and R2 time lags differ across the models
Found: the ambient noise field at one station; nothing set
R2 identification survives epoch length, RMSR_S windows, tf-PWS exponent, stacking method, bootstrap and ellipticity; the final model fits independent body-wave picks
Upper mantle slower than the mean model; S-wave LVZ to about 400 km
Not assessable: no review file supplied (acknowledgments name an editor and reviewers)

end.claim: R2 waves recovered by InSight autocorrelation yield a Martian upper mantle model slower than the Stähler et al. (2021) mean, with an S-wave low-velocity zone extending to about 400 km depth.

decisive_move.sentence: Without identifying the R2 arrival at about 6,000 s in the stacked single-station autocorrelations, there is no waveform to compare with synthetics or to invert.

gates.evidence: The data are the mission's continuous record, not collected to test a hypothesis. The model comparison could have failed: time lags change sign across the suite, and the final model is checked against independent body-wave picks (p. 5). The LVZ result itself is only checked for consistency with cited studies. Processing parameters (G = 1.02, tf-PWS power 2 'empirically', windows) were chosen without pre-registration (p. 3).

imports.item: Bootstrap resampling of the daily autocorrelations to test the robustness of the R2 identification
Monte Carlo random-perturbation search for the velocity model

limits: The Supporting Information (Figures S1-S15, Text S2, Table S1) was not supplied, so the checks reported there are coded from the main text's description only. The Monte Carlo search is small (10 models per iteration, 3 iterations) and reports no posterior or uncertainty, so 'estimate_with_resolution' is generous: resolution is implied only by sensitivity kernels (Figure S12) and uncertainty is not quantified. Non-uniqueness of the single-path R2 fit is not discussed. The inversion is 1-D and uses a single station. Sub-claims: R2 is recoverable from InSight noise autocorrelation (capability_characterized, supported by robustness tests); the upper mantle is slower than the Stähler et al. mean (best_explanation among the model suite); LVZ consistency with the shadow zone and laboratory data (best_explanation, from cited work). The glitch-origin critique of the authors' earlier PcP observation is deferred to another manuscript. Inference: the paper went through review (an editor and two reviewers are acknowledged), but what review changed cannot be seen.
